articles.title: I used to read TV audiences live. Now I read app reviews the same way.
articles.excerpt: In 2013 I worked as an applied anthropologist at a market research firm in Mexico City. One of my jobs: when a TV network premiered a telenovela, I watched the audience, not the show. While each episo…
articles.body: In 2013 I worked as an applied anthropologist at a market research firm in Mexico City. One of my jobs: when a TV network premiered a telenovela, I watched the audience, not the show. While each episode aired, I followed what people wrote on social media in real time. How they felt about the characters and the story, and how that changed from scene to scene. The network learned how people felt while it was still happening, not weeks later in a survey. That method has a name: netnography , ethnography of online communities. Thirteen years later, now as a frontend engineer, I used it again for a UX case study on a Mexican mobile carrier. No TV this time: 55 public comments from app stores and a Facebook community. It turned out to be the most useful research I did in the whole project.
articles.author: Karen Molina

articles.title: A vs B: Edge WAF vs Final Proxy Placement for HTTP Request Smuggling Defense
articles.excerpt: An API gateway returns a timeout, but the application records a request that the gateway never logged. Another client receives an unexpected response. These symptoms can indicate HTTP request smugglin…
articles.body: An API gateway returns a timeout, but the application records a request that the gateway never logged. Another client receives an unexpected response. These symptoms can indicate HTTP request smuggling: two HTTP processors disagree about where one request ends and the next begins. For security owners dealing with automated API abuse and attempts to reach privileged endpoints, this is a boundary problem worth investigating. Attackers can automate framing probes across exposed routes, looking for a proxy chain that interprets their traffic inconsistently. The practical question is how to stop http request smuggling at the proxy layer without assuming that adding a WAF automatically resolves parsing differences.
articles.author: 禾

articles.title: How to Stop HTTP Request Smuggling at the Proxy Layer: A Setup and Verification Guide
articles.excerpt: HTTP request smuggling exploits a disagreement between servers about where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. For security owners investigating API abuse or possible account takeover, that dis…
articles.body: HTTP request smuggling exploits a disagreement between servers about where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. For security owners investigating API abuse or possible account takeover, that disagreement matters: an attacker may cause a backend to process a request that the frontend did not recognize as a separate request. Depending on the architecture, consequences can include access-control bypass or interference with another user's traffic. If you are researching how to stop http request smuggling at the proxy layer, start with request framing across the entire delivery path. Adding a WAF provides a place to inspect traffic, but it does not by itself prove that every proxy and backend interprets requests consistently.
articles.author: Lia

articles.title: Your fetch() Was Aborted. The Server Still Committed the Work？
articles.excerpt: A rejected fetch() promise does not tell you whether the server changed anything. In a small local experiment, the client received AbortError, the server noticed the disconnected response, and the ser…
articles.body: A rejected fetch() promise does not tell you whether the server changed anything. In a small local experiment, the client received AbortError , the server noticed the disconnected response, and the server's simulated write still completed. Adding a server cancellation handler prevented pending work. Moving the write earlier made cancellation too late. Those three outcomes can look identical in a client log. The result worth testing Five scenarios ran five times each. Every run asserted both the client outcome and the final server counter: 25 scenario checks passed . Here, “commit” means incrementing an in-memory counter. It does not mean a database transaction.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.

articles.title: New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra
articles.excerpt: A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound. Four new sonifications use data of stars that are a…
articles.body: 4 Min Read New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound. Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and young stars are present, astronomers can better understand the lifecycle of all stars, including our own Sun. NASA/CXC/SAO/K.Arcand, SYSTEM Sounds (M. Russo, A. Santaguida M82 The galaxy Messier 82 (M82) is called a starburst galaxy because stars are forming there at a rate tens or even hundreds of times higher than in our Milky Way galaxy.

articles.title: 'Neuromancer:' Release date, cast & everything we know about Apple TV's new cyberpunk series
articles.excerpt: Hack into our handy guide to this electrifying adaptation of William Gibson’s cult ‘80s novel.
articles.body: We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's " Blade Runner 2099 " is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with " Neuromancer " blasting onto Apple TV. Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.
